the customer makes an application for a non cost share element of Access to Work (AtW) and then makes a subsequent application for either APE, SAE or Miscellaneous support.

2. Mandatory cost share doesn’t apply to applications for APE, SAE or Miscellaneous support where the customer has been in paid employment for less than 6 weeks. In these cases, any costs would be met by AtW in full.

3. Where mandatory cost share would otherwise apply, it will be waived when the adviser has identified that funding for SAE falls under the Tech Fund provision.

Note: The Tech Fund provision only applies to SAE.

Cost share applies

4. There are 4 categories of employers:

Category of employer Number of employees Employer contribution threshold

Micro 1 to 9 Nil cost share

Small 10 to 49 Nil cost share

Medium 50 to 249 £500

Large 250+ £1,000

5. Where cost share applies, there is a threshold below which AtW pays none of the cost.

6. There’s a £10,000 ceiling below which AtW pays up to 80% of the approved costs and above which AtW pays all the costs over the 3 year AtW period.

For example:

calculation Cost

Total figure that attracts cost share (Item cost) £14,000

Minus the threshold a large employer pays -£1,000

Total = £13,000

20% of cost share applicable amount for employers contribution (AtW will pay the 80%) £10,000 x 20%

This equals = £2,000

Add the threshold back in + £1,000

Final total for large employer contribution over a 3 year award = £3,000

7. Don’t include voluntary workers or take into account the number of hours an employee works when calculating the number of employees.

Note: If the customer works for an international company, you must only consider the total number of employees based in sites in Great Britain when identifying the category of the employer.

Recording application details

8. You must identify the size of the employer by recording micro, small, medium or large in the notes space within the system. Change the cost share status if necessary.

9. In all cases, you must enter the cost share marker status and AtW start date on the appropriate IT system.

10. Details of the AtW application history must always be recorded in the customer’s case. This ensures there’s a record of cumulative costs paid by the employer in repeat applications within the 3 year AtW period.

11. Once the 3 year AtW period ends, the cost sharing period starts again.

Franchises

12. A franchise is a right given to an individual or group, to market or sell a company’s goods or services within a certain area or location.

13. An individual or group who purchases a franchise is called a franchisee.

14. It’s the franchisee who is the employer and not the company whose goods or services are being marketed or sold.

15. You must establish the total number of people employed by the franchisee when considering cost share. (They may run more than one site).

16. If there’s still doubt after contacting the franchisee, you must use your discretion. Generally the benefit of doubt should be given to the franchisee.

Calculating the threshold and ceiling

17. The thresholds include VAT even if the employer may be able to claim it back at a later date.

18. Any contribution made by an employer, including voluntary contributions, must be deducted from the total cost before any mandatory cost share is calculated.

19. You mustn’t take into account any costs the employer met before the application was made.

20. Only apply one threshold where AtW support benefits a number of individuals. For example, improved building access for several disabled employees.

21. A threshold per person must be applied in cases of bulk applications for equipment.

Note: For all calculations, you must round down.

Order of deductions

22. Follow the order bulleted below for any deductions:

deduct the NHS voucher /Personal Wheelchair Budget (PWB) from the full cost

deduct any voluntary employer contribution

deduct any Tech Fund contribution (if applicable) Note: this applies to steps 4 and 5 only. Not step 6 - see scenario 4 and scenario 5

deduct the appropriate employer threshold

deduct 20% employer mandatory cost share

deduct the social and domestic contribution based on the number of non-working days that the applicant benefits from the item, for example 2/7

the remaining balance is the AtW contribution

For Example:

Maximum mandatory cost share example

Calculation Medium Employer Large Employer

Item Cost £15,000 £15,000

Deduct threshold £500 £1,000

Balance after threshold deducted £14,500 £14,000

Cost Share applicable amount £10,000 £10,000

20% of cost share applicable amount £2,000 £2,000

Total employer cost (Threshold and Cost Share) £2,500 £3,000

ATW cost £12,500 £12,000

Mid value example

Calculation Medium Employer Large Employer

Item Cost £5,000 £5,000

Deduct threshold £500 £1,000

Balance after threshold deducted £4,500 £4,000

Cost Share applicable amount £4,500 £4,000

20% of cost share applicable amount £900 £800

Total employer cost (Threshold and Cost Share) £1,400 £1,800

ATW cost £3,600 £3,200

Lower value example

Calculation Medium Employer Large Employer

Item Cost £1,100 £1,100

Deduct threshold £500 £1,000

Balance after threshold deducted £600 £100

Cost Share applicable amount £600 £100

20% of cost share applicable amount £120 £20

Total employer cost (Threshold and Cost Share) £620 £1,020

ATW cost £480 £80

Note: Following the step-by-step worked examples below will ensure that your calculations are accurate and satisfy policy intent. All calculations must be rounded down.

passages.quote:
ered with Companies House.

HM Revenue and Customs checks for self-employment

12. You can rely on HM Revenue and Customs treatment of the customer’s employment circumstances. This ensures consistency when determining an applicant is self-employed.

if the customer is employed, they will be taxed under PAYE rules and the employer will pay Class1 National Insurance contributions under the same PAYE rules

if the customer is self-employed, customers will be taxed under the Self-Assessment rules and have a UTR number for that purpose. Customers will be managing their Class 2/4 contributions through arrangements with the HMRC National Insurance Contributions Office

Business viability

13. It’s a requirement for a self-employed person or business owner/director seeking AtW support, to demonstrate that the business is a viable and legitimate concern.

14. To be considered viable, a business should achieve a minimum level of turnover each year in the course of normal operations.

15. This minimum level is set as the Lower Earnings Limit (LEL):

the LEL for 2026 to 2027 - £6,708

the LEL for 2025 to 2026 - £6,500

the LEL for 2024 to 2025 - £6,396

the LEL for 2023 to 2024 - £6,396

the LEL for 2022 to 2023 - £6,396

the LEL for 2021 to 2022 - £6,240

the LEL for 2020 to 2021 - £6,240

the LEL for 2019 to 2020 - £6,136

the LEL for 2018 to 2019 - £6,032

the LEL for 2017 to 2018 - £5,876

Refer to: GOV.UK Rates and Allowances for current or previous LEL. This site includes previous years rates.

Start-up period and down-turns

16. Any new application must be accompanied by a business plan. Advisers may decline any self-employment award if, in their judgement, the plan is unlikely to have any prospect of becoming viable.

17. New businesses or periods of sole trading may have an initial 3-year period of “test trading” where they do not have to achieve turnover at the LEL threshold.

18. Awards must be reviewed after the end of year 3 (when the first 2 years’ accounts would be available) with the view to achieving LEL in year 3.

19. If turnover has achieved LEL during the first 2 years of the test trading period, then a renewal award can be made for 3 years.

20. If LEL turnover has not been achieved during the first 2 years but progress has been made towards achieving it, and there are realistic prospects that turnover will reach the required level in year 3, a further award of 12 months can be made.

21. The customer must be made aware that if LEL turnover isn’t achieved in year 3 or in the 12 month award the award will not be renewed.

Note: Subject to satisfying all other criteria Case Managers should agree a 3 year award for a new business. When renewing after 3 years, customers will need to submit their accounts or tax returns so case managers can check turnover achieved in the second year of trading to determine continued business viability. Viable businesses should then have annual reviews to determine continued business viability.

22. An award must be terminated if self–employed trading or, a business previously not satisfying the viability test, fails to achieve turnover of the LEL in between annual review periods.

Note: This does not apply to test trading periods.

23. If a previously viable business fails to achieve turnover of LEL in between annual review periods, then a further award may be made for the following year. If the business then fails to turnover the LEL in that following year, then the award is terminated.

24. Periods for which an award is suspended, for example through temporary cessation of trading is disregarded. For example, bereavement.

Requalification

25. A person who receives an award for AtW on a self-employed basis which is subsequently terminated because the business does not satisfy the viability test, may not re-qualify for another self-employment AtW award for a period of 5 years from the date the customer first applied and subsequently awarded funding for support.

Note: An AtW award can be considered if the customer claims self-employment as a different type of business to their previous one and satisfies all other criteria.

VAT

26. All VAT queries must be signposted to HMRC.

Foster Carers

27. Case Managers must determine whether the applicant receives money as a salary for Foster caring, or whether the money they receive is solely for the child/children.

28. If the Foster carer receives a salary and satisfies standard AtW eligibility criteria, then they can be considered for support.

29. If the money received is for the child/children, is not considered a salary. This is considered voluntary work and AtW cannot provide funding.

Self-employed contractors and freelancers, including gig economy workers

1. Contractors and freelancers, including those customers working in the ‘gig economy’, are paid for instances of work, or ‘gigs’ as opposed to receiving a predicted monthly wage. The instances of work are usually temporary job roles rather than permanent.

2. In order to be considered as self-employed within the gig economy, a customer would normally identify as a contractor or a freelancer.

Contractor

3. Contractors:

typically work for single client at any one time, usually on the client’s premises

are hired on fixed-term contracts through recruitment agencies, or directly with the end client

work on a business-to-business basis with clients, whether through an agency or otherwise. They usually work for one client at a time, often full-time on a particular project for several months

are self-employed, and responsible for paying tax through the self-assessment process

may be a sole trader or have a limited company

have full control of what work they take on

can advertise their services to get new business

set their own working hours

Note: This list is not exhaustive

Freelancer

4. Freelancers:

to recruit a new employee as a support worker

64. AtW can repay:

a full salary

national insurance contributions

pension, leave and sickness payments

recruitment costs including advertising

costs of a temporary SW to cover the sick employed SW

65. Rates of pay should be looked at again at the yearly review or if the level of support changes.

66. If the SW is off sick for a period of time and the customer is remaining in work, it’s possible to fund this via AtW and should be considered to ensure the retention of the customer’s job. It’s usual to agree to pay for the SW if they or the customer are sick for up to 4 weeks in a rolling 12-month period from the first period of sickness.

67. AtW can pay recruitment costs up to 5% of the SW’s gross salary. This covers the cost of adding the new employee to the payroll and any other HR activities. This must only be done if the employer asks for it. AtW will repay the full cost when an employer provides evidence to show that they have had to pay an amount greater than this percentage. They must provide a breakdown to demonstrate how this amount is made up.

68. Redundancy and notice payments costs can be paid. Don’t profile redundancy or notice payments into the applicant’s profile. These costs must be profiled when they occur.

69. Costs cannot be applied for retrospectively and would be unlikely to be paid if such an application was received.

70. Case Managers need to agree a fixed period for which AtW will pay to cover unexpected absences such as sick leave. This must be included in the offer letter outlining the agreed support including the number of hours and rate of pay etc.

71. If a customer accepts the responsibilities of being their SW’s employer they might need additional support to fulfil this role properly. These costs can be approved through AtW where the need is related to their disability, illness or health condition.

72. Case Managers must agree an extra number of hours initially, but keep this under review. Don’t meet this need through an increase in the hourly rate paid to the SW.

73. Customers and SWs who wish to find out their employment position must be told to contact their local HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) office.

74. HMRC has a Helpline for new employers.

Telephone: 0300 200 3211

Text phone: 0300 200 3212

75. If any financial liability is incurred as a result of a customer being considered an employer by the HMRC, Case Managers may arrange for the customer to be reimbursed from this element. In all such cases, tell the AtW policy team of the details at once.

76. Customers who use family or friends to provide SW help are equally subject to the considerations above.

Support workers booked through an agency

77. If the customer or employer wishes to use an alternative supplier, Case Managers must confirm that the rate quoted is reasonable.

78. All quotes should be a total amount, including all support, travels costs and any necessary booking fees. This allows the AtW Case Manager to see which agency offers the most cost effective solution for the entire service.

Payment for a support worker

79. Payment for a SW will only be made for the days on which a customer would usually work or for other days for example, leave written in the SW’s contract of employment.

80. These costs must be confirmed with the employer of the SW. Case Managers can now obtain details from the SW Contract verbally if the employer agrees. Case Managers will record details from the contract of employment in the Additional Info (Payment Team) field under the appropriate Element.

81. Customers or employers who do not wish to share this information by telephone can continue to post or email (if a reasonable adjustment) any Contract of employment / Time Sheet / Wage slip to Access to Work for Support Workers costs. Case managers will transfer the required contractual information into the Additional Info (Payment Team) field under the appropriate Element.

82. The following information must be checked with the SW Claim form to validate and issue payment:

Full Name of Support Worker

Number of hours worked per week

Total salary paid

Total NI & Pension contributions made

Any annual leave and/or sick leave taken during the period being claimed for

83. Payment officers must check in the Additional Info (Payment Team) field under the appropriate Element before approving/rejecting any claims.

84. Personal information should be redacted from the Timesheet / Wage slip. Only the information required to validate the claim will be used.

85. Where the SW is employed by the customer or customer’s Employer they will continue to be paid if the customer is sick for up to 4 weeks, in a 12-month period from the first period of sickness

86. Case Managers must profile all costs, inclusive of VAT, over a 52-week period as the SW may be entitled to holiday/sickness payments from the customer/employer under the Working Time Regulations introduced in October 1998.

87. Under the regulations, a worker is entitled to 5.6 weeks’ leave or at least 28 days if a person were to work a 5-day week. This isn’t in addition to contractual rights.

See: holiday entitlement on the GOV.UK website.

88. AtW will pay for these weeks leave, as it’s an extra cost that would not have been relevant had the employer or customer not needed to employ the SW.

See: Health & Safety Executive website for specific information.

See: Pay and work rights on the GOV.UK website.

See: The Working Time Regulations on the Heath and Safety Executive website.

Flexible personalisation

89. Build in a tolerance to allow for small increases in support without the need for approval of a new business case and based on need only.

90. The percentage tolerance range must be up to 5%, and must only be applied after all reasons have been included in the reaching of the yearly profile.
